label: CA firm strategy and partner management
overview: CA firm strategy engagements address the high-stakes decisions that determine the long-term shape of an accounting or advisory practice — partner admission and retirement, technology and AI adoption, capacity management, and pricing strategy. These decisions are uniquely complex because they involve both the commercial interests of the firm and the personal financial interests of individual partners. The advisor's role is to provide a structured decision framework that separates the strategic logic (what is right for the firm) from the financial negotiation (what each partner receives), ensuring both are addressed transparently and in the correct sequence.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the firm strategy challenge primarily a partner structure decision (admission, retirement, or exit), a technology and AI adoption question, a capacity and workload management problem, or a fee growth and pricing strategy issue?
diagnostic_entry.partner_structure: Partner decisions are among the most consequential and relationship-sensitive decisions in a professional services firm. The diagnostic must distinguish between planned transitions (retirement with adequate lead time), performance-driven exits (partner not meeting agreed standards), and structural changes (merger, acquisition, or partner count reduction). Each requires a different framework.
diagnostic_entry.technology_adoption: AI and software adoption decisions in CA firms are frequently under-evaluated — either dismissed without analysis or adopted reactively in response to competitor pressure. The advisor must ensure the technology case is assessed on measurable ROI (time saved, error reduction, client capability improvement) and that the change management plan is as robust as the technology selection.
diagnostic_entry.capacity_management: Most CA firms have a utilisation problem that masquerades as a staffing problem. Before recommending a hire, the advisor must establish baseline capacity, identify where hours are being lost to low-value work, and determine whether redeployment is more efficient than recruitment.
diagnostic_entry.fee_growth: Fee growth in CA firms is often constrained by the absence of a systematic pricing review, not by market resistance. The diagnostic must identify whether the firm is pricing on time (hourly billing), value (outcome-based pricing), or a hybrid — and whether the pricing model is aligned to the segments of work being delivered.

materials.name: Capacity Planner & Target Models
materials.summary: The calculators that define the logistics of delivering advisory alongside compliance — where the growth is, and what time budget each team member has given the client base and their skills. My Fee Growth Plan gets an advisor to name their target clients, service niche and marketing statement; the Team Advisory Targets table sets fee targets, client focus and time expectations so nobody is guessing what is expected of them.
materials.who_when: Firm leaders mapping total capacity, and individual advisors — on full or shared autonomy — tasked with growing a fee base.
steps: Compile the family-grouped accounts into the Capacity Planner.
Categorise every client into Growth, Maintain or Service on fee potential and importance, so time follows value rather than noise.
Have each fee-growing advisor complete the My Fee Growth Model to set their own sales activity and conversion assumptions.
Have them complete My Fee Growth Plan to define target clients, service niches and their marketing statement in their own words.
Let them finish both independently before partner review — the buy-in comes from having set the numbers themselves.
Summarise the outcome in the Team Advisory Targets table: fee target, new versus existing client focus, autonomy level, time expectation.
Use My Improvement Plan instead for internal staff who are not required to grow fees — the same plan for everyone is the wrong tool for half the team.

materials.name: Team Training O.S. & Coaching Progress Plan
materials.summary: Names the functional skills each team member needs and tailors the coaching to their experience and the firm's budget. Its distinguishing idea is scheduling: learning runs in work sprints arranged around peak workflow, which is what stops training being quietly abandoned every compliance season.
materials.who_when: Firm managers, internal coaches, and all team members.
steps: Define, per person, the functional skills that need to improve — the Team Training O.S. is a coaching outcome statement, not a wish list.
Tailor the coaching content to the individual's experience and the budget available.
Schedule the learning in work sprints built around peak workflow commitments rather than in spite of them.
Run internal training on Team AI familiarity tasks so the team can prompt AI and use basic automation.
Have people test the same input across more than one AI model and compare the outputs for bias and accuracy.
Track every hour in the CPD Table, which feeds the firm-wide learning matrix and generates association points.
Protect the Weekly Golden Hour for strategic learning, ahead of compliance delivery.

materials.name: Growth Curve Checklist
materials.summary: Aligns what the firm offers with where the client's business actually is — Design, Launch, Growth, Maturity. It is the cross-selling roadmap: it tells the advisor which service genuinely belongs in this client's plan now, such as succession planning for a mature business, and just as usefully which pitches would be irrelevant today.
steps: Review the checklist when brainstorming which service offers to align to which client lifecycle stages.
Record the client's current position on the Growth Curve during the meeting itself.
Use that position to flush out both the long-term vision and the short-term concerns.
Match the service suggestion to the stage rather than to the firm's capability — the point is relevance, not coverage.
Link the outcome into the client's action plan so the identified potential turns into scheduled work.

materials.name: Strategic Evaluation Frameworks
materials.summary: Two structured ways to make divisive firm decisions without emotion. The Technology Review evaluates software and AI through Everett Rogers' diffusion of innovation and Porter's Five Forces, which is what keeps shiny-object syndrome in check. The Offshoring Review runs the partner group through De Bono's Six Hats so facts, feelings, risks and benefits are examined separately instead of argued simultaneously.
materials.who_when: The partner group and firm directors.
steps: For a technology or AI decision, start with the diffusion curve to establish the firm's genuine adoption appetite rather than its self-image.
Apply Porter's Five Forces to the same decision to read the market pressure and the expectations that come with adopting.
For a divisive operational question such as offshoring, deploy the Six Hats framework instead.
Have the chairperson force every member to wear the same hat at the same time — white for facts, red for emotions, black for risks, yellow for benefits.
That simultaneity is the mechanism: it is what removes confirmation bias and stops the discussion becoming an argument.

materials.name: Contrast Models — FM Expectations and FM Stages
materials.summary: Described in the source as the best bang-for-buck planning tools in the set. The two tables map the interrelatedness between what the owners actually want and the sequential business development objectives required to get there — so an aspiration is followed to the work it implies rather than left as a statement of intent.
materials.who_when: Partners, directors and firm managers defining their End Game.
steps: Capture the owners' aspirations plainly, in their words, before any objective is written.
Map those aspirations against the sequential development objectives that would deliver them.
Read the interrelatedness — which objectives serve more than one aspiration, and which aspiration currently has nothing beneath it.
Use the Strategic Services Summary to decide which services to develop and which to avoid, assigning a firm champion to each.
Use the Vital Internal Functions Summary to decide which internal tasks — workflow, IT, database management — are in-house or outsourced, each with a named champion.

materials.name: Tracking & Accountability — Global Actions Report & CPD Log
materials.summary: Centralises accountability so advice becomes evidence. The Global Actions Report summarises every action promised to clients across all advisors, letting management see completion, bottlenecks and automation opportunities; the CPD Log tracks all learning. Together they answer the question a firm usually cannot: is what we advise actually getting done in the field?
materials.who_when: Firm management tracking performance, and advisors tracking their own daily commitments.
steps: Record targets, objectives and specific actions per client account in the Advisor Action Plan.
Let it set the automated reminders so nothing promised in a meeting is lost afterwards.
Run the Global Actions Report when management needs to verify that advice is turning into completed tasks.
Read it for the three things it shows: failures, automation opportunities, and genuine field effectiveness.
Use the Dashboard and Volatility Report alongside it in delivery, so financial performance can be explained to the client simply.
Keep the CPD Log current so learning is evidenced rather than asserted.

advisor_guidance.separate_strategic_and_financial_convers: Partner structure decisions always involve both a strategic logic (what is right for the firm) and a financial negotiation (what each partner receives). These conversations must be run in sequence, not simultaneously. Conflating the strategic question with the financial negotiation creates conditions where partners vote on strategy based on their financial position — undermining the quality of the decision.
advisor_guidance.technology_change_management_is_not_opti: The majority of technology adoption failures in professional services firms are change management failures, not technology failures. A rigorous selection process that is not matched by an equally rigorous implementation and behaviour change plan will produce a technology investment that is underutilised within 6-12 months.
advisor_guidance.capacity_before_recruitment: The instinct to hire when the firm feels stretched is almost always premature. Most CA firms discover through a proper capacity analysis that the constraint is in how work is deployed, not the total quantum of people. Run the utilisation and write-off analysis before approving any new headcount.
advisor_guidance.pricing_conversations_are_leadership_con: Fee growth resistance inside the firm is almost always a leadership issue, not a market issue. Advisors who are conflict-averse will find reasons why their specific clients cannot accept a fee increase. The partner group must model the pricing conversation behaviour they want to see in the advisory team.
